evidence: The SCC approved Dominion's new GS-5 large-load rate class (PUR-2025-00058, Nov 2025, 25 MW+ at 75% load factor) and an Appalachian Power large power schedule (PUR-2025-00057).
GS-5 requires 14-year contracts with minimum demand charges of 85% for transmission/distribution and 60% for generation, and customers stay liable for minimums if they exit early.
Collateral terms for GS-5 were not stated in the sources I could open; scored moderate because the class carries stranded-cost protections, but this is unverified.
pending: Check the SCC final order in PUR-2025-00058 for credit/collateral language.

evidence: The GS-5 order and the July 2026 Affordable Virginia package (signed July 1, 2026) put ratepayer protections against data-center-driven infrastructure costs into law.
pending: SB 339 cost-subsidy investigation may move in the 2027 session.

evidence: No statewide pause; localities are acting (Loudoun attorney opinion of Sept 2026 allows up to 12 months of delay, Prince William amended its overlay to largely end by-right development).
pending: Local actions are described as not technically moratoria; scored at the local level.

evidence: Siting stays with localities; Gov. Spanberger's EO 22 (Sept 18, 2026) does not change local zoning and only withholds discretionary state help.
pending: Virginia Energy siting recommendations due in 240 days.

evidence: EO 22 bars VEDP discretionary assistance (Business Ready Sites, expedited permitting) for new projects of 25 MW or more, a sub-100 MW state trigger.
pending: Trigger is loss of state assistance rather than a formal review.

evidence: No dedicated fast-track program; Loudoun reports local review could run up to 12 months from submittal.
Sales and use tax exemption is active but requires $150M investment, 50 jobs at 150% of prevailing wage and a VEDP MOU; it runs to 2035 and was preserved in the June 2026 budget (HB 30).
pending: Joint Subcommittee on Tax Policy report due Dec 15, 2026.

evidence: No state property-tax abatement program was found; localities set their own business property tax on data center equipment. Level reflects routine local treatment, not verified in this research.
The exemption requires MOU thresholds within three years and the benefit must be repaid if investment/job thresholds are not met.
No statewide data-center water reporting or limit is in effect; EO 22 only directs DEQ to build an accelerated water-rule workplan within 180 days.

HB 507 (effective July 1, 2026) requires data center air permits to meet at least Tier 4-equivalent limits; DEQ guidance sets a presumptive 0.60 g/hp-hr limit effectively requiring SCR; SB 336/HB 1502 added stricter standards.
pending: EO 22 orders cumulative-impact review of generators.

evidence: No data-center-specific or general state environmental review applying to private data centers was found.
pending: DEQ studies under EO 22 could change this.

evidence: No mandatory curtailment or on-site generation limits are in force; EO 22 only directs work on possible curtailment arrangements with the SCC and PJM.
Labor-type conditions exist only as incentive terms (jobs paying 150% of prevailing wage under the sales tax exemption MOU).
Reporting is incentive-linked through the VEDP MOU; EO 22 limits new NDAs and calls for model disclosure guidance.
No statewide noise or setback rule for data centers yet; EO 22 directs DEQ to accelerate noise rules.
pending: DEQ noise workplan due in 180 days.

evidence: Major changes are pending: EO 22 reports due in 120-240 days, a tax-policy study due Dec 15, 2026, and 2027 legislation expected.
Loudoun cites up to 12 months of local delay; broader grid interconnection backlog was not documented in the sources I could open.
pending: Dominion/PJM queue delays not independently verified here.

evidence: 2025 Next Generation Energy Act and the 2026 RELIEF Act (HB 1532) require utilities to file large-load tariffs; filings went to the PSC on Sept 1, 2026 (PC72) and are pending.
No enacted minimum-bill or term rules yet; the terms will be set in the pending PSC tariff proceedings.
No large-load-specific collateral rule is in effect; HB 1532 imposes a registration fee of at least $1,000 per MW of peak load, but that is a fee rather than collateral.
HB 1532 (Chapter 353, signed May 12, 2026) lowered the large-load definition to 25 MW/60% load factor and requires pass-through of PJM capacity costs to large-load accounts.
Many counties have local moratoria (14 of 24 jurisdictions per press); no statewide moratorium, though a GOP candidate now calls for one.
pending: Candidate calls for a statewide moratorium; none proposed by governor or legislature.

evidence: The Sept 23, 2026 EO creates a statewide review by a Data Center Accountability Task Force; projects rated Not Aligned lose state support and state review is deferred until local approvals are documented.
The EO applies to projects of 25 MW or more and to Large Load Customers.
The EO offers a Coordinated Review Pathway for Aligned projects, and HB 1532 offers accelerated permitting for a voluntary clean-capacity rating; no general timelines are documented.
A 2020 sales and use tax exemption is active with low thresholds ($2M or $5M investment depending on location); Gov. Moore plans to seek repeal in 2027.
No state property-tax abatement for data centers was found; local treatment not verified.
The sales tax exemption required job creation and minimum investment; the EO ties state incentive eligibility to Task Force alignment.
HB 1532 registration covers energy and water use, and the EO review covers water availability and cooling technology; a public dashboard will show water use.
No Maryland-specific generator limits were found; the EO folds backup-generator emissions into project review only.
The EO sets a data-center-specific review covering water, cooling, generator emissions, stormwater and Chesapeake Bay impacts.
The EO asks developers to consider curtailment or flexible-load participation; no mandate in force.
HB 1532's voluntary clean-capacity rating (with accelerated permitting) carries a prevailing wage condition for construction.
HB 1532 creates mandatory registration covering energy and water use, and the EO sets up a monthly public dashboard of location, peak demand and water use.
No statewide noise or setback rule for data centers found.
PSC large-load tariffs are pending, the EO is new, and legislative changes (including exemption repeal) are expected in 2027.
Moderate: many local moratoria and pending tariff proceedings; no documented queue figures were found.

PPL's large-load tariff was approved in its rate settlement (R-2025-3057164) and the PUC adopted a statewide model tariff framework (M-2025-3054271) for 50 MW/100 MW aggregate that is guidance, not binding.
PPL's class sets a minimum ten-year commitment; the model tariff offers non-binding guidance on minimum terms and exit provisions.
The model tariff includes deposits and financial security against stranded assets and enhanced CIAC up-front payments, but as guidance with no amounts.
The model tariff reinforces cost causation and the Aug 18, 2026 EO 2026-05 pushes the PUC to make data centers bear PJM backstop and interconnection costs; neither is yet a binding statewide mandate.
No statewide or local moratorium was confirmed in the sources reviewed.
EO 2026-05 requires local approvals and sets a two-track DEP process with consent orders and GRID requirements.
The EO's GRID requirements and consent orders apply to projects above 25 MW of peak demand.

Data centers are removed from the Permit Fast Track program; Track 1 projects get rolling review, Track 2 waits for all applications; the model tariff expects interconnection studies within six months.
The sales/use tax exemption program (Act 25 of 2021) is active but requires at least $75M investment, 25 jobs and $1M in wages, and the EO orders new GRID conditions for applicants.
pending: Revenue guidelines being updated per EO.

evidence: The state data center program does not exempt property taxes.
The exemption carries job, investment and wage conditions, and the EO adds GRID compliance; clawback terms were not confirmed.
Annual water consumption reporting to DEP is required starting July 1, 2027, and Track 2 projects need water withdrawal/discharge authorizations before review.
No state-specific generator limits yet; the EO only directs DEP to recommend rules on backup generator controls, cumulative impacts and grid use.
Data-center-specific DEP consent orders under the GRID requirements, including environmental protection terms, apply to projects of 25 MW or more.
The EO advocates PUC rules to curtail data centers first in emergencies and ties Track 1 to bringing power generation; not yet mandated.
The GRID requirements include workforce and economic development focus but no specific labor standards were found.
Operating data centers must report energy and water consumption under the Fiscal Code by July 1, 2027 and annually, per the EO.
No statewide noise or setback rules for data centers found.
The EO is new, expected to draw legal challenges, with unclear treatment of existing projects, and the model tariff is non-binding.
PJM large-load integration rules are still being revised under FERC's June 2026 order; PA-specific queue data not found.
HB 233 (signed Aug 26, 2026) requires Delmarva to create a higher rate class for hyperscale users; Delmarva's GS-LL (Docket 25-0826, 50 MW+) is still pending at the PSC.
No enacted minimum-bill or term requirement was found; GS-LL terms are pending.
No large-load-specific collateral rule found; SB 205 (certificate to operate with financial commitments) stalled in committee.
Laws signed Aug 26, 2026 bar data centers from passing costs to ratepayers, make them bear T&D and capacity costs, and require them to bring their own generation (HB 445).
No moratorium was found; critics called SB 205 a de facto moratorium but it did not advance.
State review applies through the Coastal Zone Act (DNREC and the Coastal Zone Industrial Control Board blocked Project Washington in March 2026); otherwise local approval.
No MW trigger for state review is in force (SB 205's 30 MW certificate failed; the 50 MW figure is a rate-class threshold).
No special fast-track program found; Project Washington was reviewed through a multi-month DNREC and board process.
Delaware has no general sales tax.
No state data-center property-tax abatement was found; local practices not verified.
HB 310 limits a tax credit so data centers qualify only if they bring their own generation under HB 445, and a separate measure bars job-creation credits.
The new laws do not address water use; advocates say further measures are needed.
DNREC treated 500+ diesel generators and fuel storage as prohibited heavy industry under the Coastal Zone Act, and HB 445 requires part of backup power to be clean rather than diesel.
Coastal Zone Act review applies to projects in the coastal zone, as in the Project Washington decision.
Large facilities must reduce use during peak demand and bring their own generation under the Aug 2026 laws.
No labor requirement found; job-creation tax credits are barred.
No ongoing data center operating reporting requirement found; SB 312 only bars NDAs.
No statewide noise or setback rules found.
Newly signed laws await PSC implementation, the GS-LL docket is pending, and the Project Washington developer says it still intends to proceed.
Delmarva says data centers could nearly double Delaware's power demand; no documented queue backlog.
The PSC approved Appalachian Power and Wheeling Power Large Capacity Power and Industrial Power tariffs (24-0611-E-T-PW, Mar 2025); FirstEnergy opposes a tariff and prefers special contracts.
The settlement behind the APCo large-load rules provides 12-year initial terms, about 80% purchase commitments and 100 MW minimum capacity; the order approving it was reported in Mar 2025.
pending: Final order terms not independently opened.

evidence: No collateral terms were reported for West Virginia; advocates in the FirstEnergy case want collateral but FirstEnergy refuses.
HB 2014 bars utilities from passing microgrid-related costs to other customers; broader ratepayer protections were described as lacking.
No moratorium found.
HB 2014 limits local governments from restricting microgrid districts and high-impact data centers, pointing to preemption of local limits.
The 90 MW 'high-impact' definition triggers local preemption, not extra state review.
DEP granted an air permit for a large microgrid/data center project about five months after application; HB 2014 microgrid districts are meant to streamline siting.
No data-center sales tax exemption program was identified in the sources reviewed.
pending: Not verified; no search found a program.

No incentive conditions identified because no incentives were found.
No state water requirement for data centers; large facilities can use 3-5 million gallons per day.
DEP uses its normal air permits; diesel backup concerns exist but no data-center-specific limits.
No data-center-specific or general state environmental review identified.
No curtailment mandate or limits on on-site generation; HB 2014 encourages microgrids and self-generation.
No labor conditions found.
HB 2014 shields developers from sharing certain project information; no operating reporting identified.
No statewide noise/setback rules; noise concerns raised locally.
PSC coal-capacity rules under HB 2014 head to the legislature in 2027, and the FirstEnergy gas plant case is unresolved.
